followUpQuestions.prompt: Why can’t each limiter server just keep its own counts in memory?
expectedAnswerPoints: Each server sees only part of a client’s traffic.
A client could exceed the limit by spreading requests across servers.
A shared store, or routing a client to one server, keeps the count consistent.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Compare a token bucket with a fixed window counter.
expectedAnswerPoints: A fixed window is simple but allows a burst at the boundary between two windows.
A token bucket permits controlled bursts while enforcing an average rate.
Sliding windows are more precise but cost more memory or computation.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Should the limiter fail open or fail closed when its counter store is down?
expectedAnswerPoints: Fail-open keeps the service available but removes protection.
Fail-closed protects the service but blocks legitimate users.
The right choice depends on what the limiter protects and the cost of abuse versus downtime.

referenceSolutions.name: Shared-counter limiter in front of the service

flows.name: Check a request
steps: Client sends a request through the load balancer.
The limiter looks up the client’s limit in the rules database.
The limiter atomically increments the client’s count in the shared counter store.
Under the limit: the request is forwarded to the application server.
Over the limit: the limiter returns 429 Too Many Requests.

strengths: Every request is checked before reaching the service.
Counts are shared, so adding limiter servers stays accurate.
limitations: The counter store is a dependency whose failure must be handled.
Each check adds a network round trip.
Very hot clients can concentrate load on one counter.
tradeoffs: Accuracy (shared state) versus extra latency per request.

revisionRecommendations.text: Review where cross-cutting checks belong in a request path (edge, gateway or service).
Review shared state, atomic counters and consistency across servers.
Review capacity planning and how per-request checks add latency.
Review failure modes: fail-open versus fail-closed trade-offs.
